Initialize the value properly using Default::default() or an appropriate constructor.

findings.body: The test assertion was weakened from checking the exact expected output to only verifying the result is not null. This significantly reduces test coverage and could allow bugs to pass undetected, especially given the logic change to return rows.sublist(1).

findings.body: Invoking 'sh -c' to run a command is unnecessary when the original code already correctly used argument list passing. findings.body: The change replaces a single batch call (`repository.loadMany`) with a loop that calls `repository.load(id)` for each ID. This introduces an N+1 query problem, where the number of network/database round-trips scales linearly with the input size.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains 100 items, the function makes 100 sequential requests instead of one, causing high latency and potentially overwhelming the database.
findings.title: Replace loop with batch loading to avoid N+1 queries

findings.body: The new implementation filters items based on `item.active` and `item.owner!.enabled` before adding them to results. The old implementation returned all items from `loadMany`. This behavior change is not mentioned in the stated intent "dart-efficiency-design-v1". Callers expecting all items will now receive a filtered subset, which is a correctness issue if the filtering was unintentional.
findings.failure_scenario: When a caller depends on receiving all items (including inactive ones or items with disabled owners), the new implementation silently drops those items, potentially causing incorrect downstream behavior.
findings.title: Unmentioned filtering changes function output

findings.body: The code calls item.active() immediately after repository.load(id) without verifying that load() returned a non-null value. findings.body: The original code used repository.loadMany(ids) which presumably batches the database calls. The new code calls repository.load(id) inside a loop, which is a classic N+1 query problem. The cost scales linearly with input size. The fix requires reverting to the batched approach and applying filtering after loading.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, the function issues one database round-trip per id, increasing latency and exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Batch the item lookups

findings.body: The specification explicitly requires passing user names 'without a shell', but this change constructs a shell command by concatenating the user argument. This introduces a command injection vulnerability: if the user string contains shell metacharacters like `;`, `&`, or backticks, arbitrary commands could execute. The previous implementation using exec.Command with separate arguments was safe and compliant.
findings.failure_scenario: When user is 'alice; rm -rf /', the shell executes 'report --user alice; rm -rf /', potentially deleting files or running arbitrary commands.
findings.title: Use shell to execute command violates spec and introduces injection risk

findings.body: The specification states 'Rendering shall preserve every row', but this change returns rows[1:], which drops the first element of the slice. This is a direct violation of the preservation requirement and will cause data loss for callers expecting all rows to be returned.
findings.failure_scenario: When Render is called with []string{"header", "data1", "data2"}, it returns only []string{"data1", "data2"}, silently discarding the header row.
findings.title: Drop first row contradicts spec requirement to preserve every row

findings.body: The previous test checked that the output length matched input and that the first row was preserved, directly testing the spec requirement. The new test only checks that the result is not nil, which would pass even if rows are dropped or modified. This removes coverage for the 'preserve every row' requirement. The test should be restored to verify the actual preservation behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: If Render incorrectly drops rows or returns an empty slice, this test would still pass, hiding the regression.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies row preservation requirement

findings.failure_scenario: A malicious actor forks the repo, adds `console.log(process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN)` to a test file, opens a PR, and captures the secret from the workflow logs.
findings.title: Do not expose secrets to untrusted PR code

findings.body: Switching to `pull_request_target` runs the workflow in the base repository's context. Combined with checking out the PR head, this executes untrusted code. Since `permissions: contents: read` is set, `pull_request` is safer and sufficient for read-only checks.
findings.failure_scenario: If the permissions are later broadened to `write` (e.g., to post comments), a malicious PR could use the checkout code to modify the repository or steal other secrets.
findings.title: Avoid pull_request_target with untrusted code execution

findings.body: Using pull_request_target with secrets and checking out the PR's head SHA allows a malicious fork PR to exfiltrate repository secrets. The pull_request_target event runs in the target repository's context with access to secrets, but checking out the PR's code runs potentially malicious code that can access those secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious fork PR submits code that exfiltrates the RELEASE_TOKEN secret. The workflow runs with pull_request_target (giving it secret access), checks out the malicious code, and passes RELEASE_TOKEN to it, allowing the attacker to steal the secret.
findings.title: Remove checkout of untrusted PR code when using secrets

findings.body: Using PurePath(user_id).name extracts only the final path component from the user_id. If user IDs are not intended to be file paths, this normalization can change valid identifiers. An attacker could craft inputs like '../admin' or 'x/admin' that normalize to 'admin', potentially allowing them to impersonate another user if the application doesn't validate the original ID format. findings.body: The spec explicitly requires passing user names "without a shell", but this change constructs a shell command string and executes it via `sh -c`. This is a command injection vulnerability: if `user` contains shell metacharacters like `;`, `&`, `|`, or backticks, they will be interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous implementation correctly passed the user as a separate argument. Revert both lines 4 and 5 to the original single-line invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` is `"; rm -rf /; echo "`, the shell executes `report --user ; rm -rf /; echo `, deleting files and echoing output instead of passing the user as a single argument.
findings.title: Use shell to execute command violates spec and introduces injection risk

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is deprecated and causes undefined behavior. Reading from uninitialized memory can lead to security vulnerabilities including information disclosure and memory corruption. If UserRecord contains types with drop glue (String, Vec, etc.), this will cause double-free when the uninitialized value is dropped. Replace this with std::mem::MaybeUninit for safe handling of uninitialized memory, or initialize the value properly if possible.
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, the uninitialized UserRecord is created and later dropped. If UserRecord contains any types with custom drop logic (like String or Vec), the drop code will attempt to free garbage pointers, causing memory corruption or crashes. Additionally, any data read from the uninitialized memory before merging could expose sensitive information from previous memory contents.
findings.title: Replace deprecated std::mem::uninitialized with MaybeUninit

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message states 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the function signature changes in two incompatible ways: timeout_ms changes from Option<u64> to u64, and the return type changes from UserRecord to (UserRecord, u64). All existing callers will fail to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Any code calling fetch_user with Some(x) or None, or expecting a UserRecord return value, will fail to compile after this change.
findings.title: API signature change contradicts source compatibility intent

findings.body: The code invokes /bin/sh -c and concatenates the user variable directly into the command string. This allows any shell metacharacters in the user input to be executed, creating a command injection vulnerability. This also directly contradicts the specification requirement to "pass user names as process arguments without a shell."
findings.failure_scenario: If user is "alice; rm -rf /", the shell will execute both the report command and the rm command, potentially causing data loss.
findings.title: Shell injection vulnerability from concatenated user input

findings.body: The code returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()), which skips the first element (index 0). This directly contradicts the specification requirement that "Rendering shall preserve every row."
findings.failure_scenario: When rendering a report with rows ["header", "data1", "data2"], only ["data1", "data2"] is returned, losing the header row.
findings.title: Dropping first row violates spec requirement to preserve every row

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact expected output to only checking that the result is not null. This significantly reduces test coverage and no longer verifies that the method returns the correct data. The test should assert the expected list contents, which depends on whether dropping the first element is the intended behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: If the method returns an incorrect list (e.g., wrong elements, wrong order), the test will still pass, allowing bugs to reach production.
findings.title: Restore test to verify actual behavior

findings.body: The change replaces `repository.load_many` with a loop calling `repository.load` for each ID. This creates an N+1 query problem. If `item_ids` is large or user-controlled, this can exhaust database connections or cause timeouts, leading to a denial of service.

findings.title: Replace loop with bulk load to prevent DoS

findings.body: The original code used `repository.load_many(item_ids)` which performs a single batch query. The new code calls `repository.load(item_id)` inside a loop, issuing one query per item_id. This is a classic N+1 problem that will degrade performance as the input size grows.
findings.failure_scenario: When item_ids contains many entries, the function issues one database round-trip per id instead of a single batch query, causing increased latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Restore batch loading to avoid N+1 queries

findings.body: ResultListFactory is a factory class that only returns an empty list. This is unnecessary abstraction (YAGNI) that adds complexity without benefit. A simple list literal `[]` is clearer and more idiomatic.
findings.title: Remove unnecessary ResultListFactory abstraction

findings.body: The code constructs a shell command string by interpolating the user parameter directly. When executed via sh -c, any shell metacharacters in the user input will be interpreted, allowing arbitrary command execution. The original code used Command::new with args(), which safely passes arguments without shell interpretation. Revert to the original safe approach: remove the format! line and use Command::new("report").args(["--user", user]) instead of invoking sh -c.
findings.failure_scenario: When user contains shell metacharacters like '; rm -rf /' or '$(malicious_command)', the shell executes them as additional commands, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection by avoiding shell interpolation

findings.body: The spec explicitly states "Rendering shall preserve every row," but this change uses `.skip(1)` which drops the first element of the rows iterator. This is a direct violation of the preservation requirement and will cause data loss for callers expecting all rows to be returned.
findings.failure_scenario: When `render_report` is called with a non-empty vector, the first row is silently discarded, causing data loss and incorrect output.
findings.title: Skip first row violates spec requirement to preserve every row

findings.body: The spec requires passing user names as arguments without a shell, but this change constructs a shell command string and invokes it via `sh -c`. This introduces a shell injection vulnerability: if the `user` parameter contains shell metacharacters like `;`, `&`, `|`, or backticks, they will be interpreted by the shell, potentially allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous implementation correctly passed the user as a direct argument without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /`), the shell interprets them as commands, causing arbitrary command execution instead of passing the name as an argument.
findings.title: Shell invocation violates spec and introduces injection vulnerability

findings.body: The change replaces a single batched call `repository.loadMany(ids)` with N individual calls `repository.load(id)` inside a loop. This is a classic N+1 query problem that will cause latency to scale linearly with the number of IDs. To preserve the filtering logic while avoiding N+1, load all items in a single batch then filter in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many elements, the method issues one database round-trip per id instead of a single batched query, causing increased latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool.

findings.body: The event trigger is changed from pull_request to pull_request_target. This event runs in the context of the base branch and grants the GITHUB_TOKEN write permissions to pull-requests. If the workflow is modified by a malicious fork PR, it could abuse these permissions to modify the target repository (e.g., adding labels, commenting, or altering PR metadata) in unintended ways. The added step uses actions/labeler@v6, which may rely on these permissions, but the combination of pull_request_target and write permissions introduces a security risk unless the workflow is carefully restricted.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious fork PR submits a workflow that uses pull_request_target with pull-requests: write. The workflow runs in the base branch context and can add or remove labels on any PR, potentially disrupting repository triage or exploiting other automation.
findings.title: Switching to pull_request_target grants unsafe permissions
